records.design: Anatomical review of the human retinal photoreceptor mosaic
records.summary: Ahnelt describes how human rods and cones are distributed across the retina. Cone packing is especially dense near the fovea; different cone populations have different arrangements. This provides biological context for exploring local packing and sampling geometry in Vision Atlas.
records.limitation: The review does not demonstrate a universal perfect hexagonal retina, tetrahedral visual processing, or a Fibonacci mechanism. It is anatomical evidence, not an EMDR treatment trial or a quantum-stability experiment.
records.mechanism: Spatial sampling by retinal photoreceptor populations.
records.researchLead: Compare the Atlas geometry with measured local packing, density and irregularity; retain the differences between retinal regions.

records.design: Computational model with comparative visual-cortex observations
records.summary: Paik and Ringach propose that interference between regularly spaced ON- and OFF-centre retinal ganglion-cell mosaics helps form orientation maps in visual cortex. Their model predicts hexagonal organisation of orientation-domain centres, with supporting patterns reported in four mammalian species.
records.limitation: This is a proposed developmental mechanism with supporting observations. It does not establish that all visual cortex follows this model, that humans prefer hexagons, or that retinal geometry stabilises quantum information.
records.mechanism: Moiré interference between two spatial mosaics.
records.researchLead: Test whether similar interference mathematics generates useful candidate patterns in the Atlas, then evaluate each physical system separately.

records.design: Human fMRI during controlled visual tracking
records.summary: Nau and colleagues found a sixfold directional pattern in human entorhinal-cortex activity during a visual tracking task. The result supports a grid-like representation of visual space and gives Vision Atlas a measured example of sixfold organisation in brain activity.
records.limitation: An fMRI population signal is not a direct image of individual grid cells or proof of a tetrahedral eye mechanism. This study does not test Fibonacci sequences, EMDR outcomes, or quantum error correction.
records.mechanism: Sixfold rotational modulation of a population-level neural signal with gaze direction.
records.researchLead: Use explicit rotational-symmetry tests with competing periodicities and independent data, rather than judging a pattern by visual resemblance.

records.summary: Hastings and Haah construct a honeycomb code in which a repeating schedule of two-qubit measurements creates logical qubits. Information protection comes from the code and measurement sequence acting together on the lattice.
records.limitation: The paper does not show that a passive hexagon alone protects information. Implementing this code requires the specified measurements and decoding; the current Aquila workflow does not implement that procedure.
records.mechanism: Dynamically generated logical qubits through scheduled two-qubit Pauli measurements.
records.researchLead: Use the measurement schedule as a separate theoretical benchmark; distinguish logical error correction from longer physical-qubit coherence.

records.title: The Penrose Tiling is a Quantum Error-Correcting Code
records.summary: Li and Boyle construct quantum error-correcting codes from Penrose tilings and variants based on Ammann–Beenker and Fibonacci tilings. Their construction connects nonperiodic geometric structure with the ability to recover information after local errors or erasures.
records.limitation: This is a mathematical construction in a preprint, not an experimental demonstration on Aquila. Its Fibonacci tilings are different from the Atlas M9 P24 sequences. A physical implementation and its resource requirements remain separate questions.
records.mechanism: Quantum information stored in a tiling-based code with local indistinguishability and recoverability.
records.researchLead: Study the explicit Fibonacci-tiling code and compare its mathematical requirements with our sequence representations before proposing a hardware mapping.

records.title: The IBM Quantum heavy hex lattice
records.authors: Paul Nation; Hanhee Paik; Andrew Cross; Zaira Nazario
records.summary: IBM explains why its heavy-hex architecture uses a sparse pattern of superconducting-qubit connections. The design reduces frequency collisions and unwanted effects on neighbouring qubits while balancing connectivity and the operations required by a calculation.
records.limitation: This is a vendor technical explanation, not a peer-reviewed Fibonacci study. Its benefits depend on superconducting hardware and control choices; the shape alone is not evidence of universal quantum stability.
records.mechanism: Reduced connectivity to manage frequency collisions and spectator errors.
records.researchLead: Compare connectivity, noise and operation overhead explicitly when evaluating alternative geometries.

records.summary: The authors combine surface-code layouts and pulse control on IBM heavy-hex processors. Increasing code size along one direction improves protection of particular logical states. Their analysis shows why both state directions and coherent noise matter when assessing error suppression.
records.limitation: Directional improvements do not establish general below-threshold scaling. The paper identifies further noise reduction needed for balanced scaling. It does not test Fibonacci or M9 P24 sequences.
records.mechanism: Code embedding, SWAP operations and dynamical decoupling on a constrained hardware graph.
records.researchLead: Evaluate several initial states and an information-preservation metric; avoid declaring success from one favourable response or direction.

records.summary: The authors assembled a molecular diatomic kagome lattice and observed electronic states along its zigzag edges. Microscopy and calculations connect these states to the lattice's electronic structure and topology.
records.limitation: This is a quantum-materials result, not a demonstration of a longer-lived qubit or an error-correcting computer. It provides an example of geometry changing electronic behaviour, without establishing a Fibonacci mechanism.
records.mechanism: Topological electronic edge states in a molecular lattice.
records.researchLead: Compare edge and bulk observables in an explicitly defined Hamiltonian; treat this as a materials analogy until a quantum-information observable is tested.

records.design: Numerical modelling and analysis of Rydberg-atom measurements
records.summary: Cong and colleagues use local error-correction ideas to identify topological order despite noise. They test the method numerically and apply it to measurements from a Rydberg-atom quantum spin liquid, making it directly relevant to analysing neutral-atom experiments.
records.limitation: The method improves the diagnosis of a prepared state. It is not a demonstration that Aquila stores arbitrary information fault-tolerantly, and it does not test M9 P24 sequences.
records.mechanism: Locally error-corrected decoration of measured correlations to identify topological order.
records.researchLead: Investigate whether the required correlation measurements and state preparation are available in our neutral-atom model before adopting the diagnostic.

records.summary: Haah constructs local stabilizer codes in three dimensions without string-like logical operators. The work introduces a different geometric organisation of information and errors, associated with the fractal structure of logical operations in the cubic-code family.
records.limitation: This is code theory, not evidence that any fractal pattern stabilises a physical quantum computer. It does not demonstrate a Fibonacci connection or a complete self-correcting memory operating at finite temperature.
records.mechanism: Three-dimensional local constraints and non-string logical operators.
records.researchLead: Compare exact code properties and noise response before drawing connections between fractal appearance and information protection.
